note: HL05 chapter capability ledger. Authored intent, not a derived cache: no validator may rewrite this file. Every declared book chapter now has an authored capability. Legacy schema-v1 entries anchor their payoff to real canonical lesson content but intentionally keep assesses empty until typed knowledge atoms exist, preserving measurable debt without inventing atoms. Chapter generation status remains independently controlled by core/book-generation.json.

chapters.title: Hola and Buenos Días
chapters.label: ch:first-words
chapters.canDo: I can greet someone in Spanish, say how I am, and wish them a good day.

payoff.summary: A short doorway greeting: hola, an answer to how you are, and buenos días on the way in.

chapters.title: The Rest of the Greetings
chapters.label: ch:greetings
chapters.canDo: I can greet someone correctly at any hour — morning, afternoon, or night.

payoff.summary: The same greeting exchange run three times across the day, choosing the right form for each hour.

chapters.title: Introducing Yourself
chapters.label: ch:introductions
chapters.canDo: I can give my name, ask someone else's, and say it was a pleasure to meet them.

payoff.summary: A first meeting start to finish: greet, exchange names at the right level of formality, and close with mucho gusto.

chapters.title: How Are You?
chapters.label: ch:how-are-you
chapters.canDo: I can ask how someone is in Spanish, formally or informally, answer for myself, and hand the question back.

payoff.summary: The whole how-are-you exchange run twice — ¿Cómo está usted? for a stranger, ¿Cómo estás? for a friend — answered with bien, regular or más o menos and closed with gracias / de nada.

chapters.title: Farewells
chapters.label: ch:farewells
chapters.canDo: I can close a Spanish conversation and pick the goodbye that fits how soon I will see the person again.

payoff.summary: One conversation from hola to its ending, choosing hasta luego, hasta mañana, hasta pronto or the final adiós to match when the two of you will next meet.

chapters.title: The First Verbs
chapters.label: ch:first-verbs
chapters.canDo: I can build my own Spanish sentences with -ar verbs and ask politely for a coffee.

payoff.summary: Conjugate hablar, trabajar and estudiar across yo, tú and usted with no pronoun spoken, answer ¿Hablas español? about yourself, then order café, por favor and run the gracias / de nada loop.

chapters.title: Eating, Drinking, Living --- the -er and -ir Verbs
chapters.label: ch:er-ir-verbs
chapters.canDo: I can use the singular forms of regular Spanish -er and -ir verbs to ask and answer what someone eats or drinks and where they live.

payoff.summary: Ask and answer a short exchange about eating, drinking, studying, and where someone lives, using the three singular regular verb patterns and only previously introduced words.

chapters.title: Numbers, and How Old You Are
chapters.label: ch:numbers-and-age
chapters.canDo: I can count from one through ten and use singular forms of tener to ask and answer age with a number I know.

payoff.summary: Count from one through ten, move among tengo, tienes, and tiene, then ask and answer age with the number frame taught in the chapter.

chapters.title: Ser and Estar --- Two Ways to Be
chapters.label: ch:ser-y-estar
chapters.canDo: I can identify someone, state origin, check wellbeing, and give a location by choosing a learned singular form of ser or estar.

payoff.summary: Identify Ana, state an origin with soy de, check a current state, and locate Ana with está en using only previously introduced vocabulary and singular forms.

chapters.title: Going, and the Future You Can Already Say
chapters.label: ch:ir-y-futuro
chapters.canDo: I can ask where someone is going, say what a singular person is going to do, and mark a known singular noun with mi, tu, or su.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C10-practice, the canonical closing checkpoint, and demonstrate the chapter promise with singular ir, ir a plus a known infinitive, and mi, tu, or su before café.
payoff.note: The payoff retrieves all nine Chapter-10 atoms and deliberately stays on the singular-person, known-infinitive, and known-noun frontier.

chapters.title: Verbs That Break in the Middle --- the Stem Changers
chapters.label: ch:stem-changes
chapters.canDo: I can express singular wanting and ability, compare the learned e-to-ie and o-to-ue changes, and say our with a known singular noun.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C11-practice, the canonical closing checkpoint, and demonstrate singular querer and poder, the learned vowel-change contrast, and nuestro or nuestra before a known singular noun.
payoff.note: The payoff retrieves all eleven Chapter-11 atoms and deliberately leaves plural persons, plural possessive agreement, and untaught nouns for later lessons.

chapters.title: Hacer, Decir, and the -go Verb Club
chapters.label: ch:yo-go-verbs
chapters.canDo: I can use the three learned singular forms of hacer and decir and compare tengo, hago, and digo without predicting unseen verbs.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C12-practice, the canonical closing checkpoint, and demonstrate the chapter promise with known words and only the learned singular person frame.
payoff.note: The payoff retrieves all eight Chapter-12 atoms and deliberately leaves plural persons, weather and homework vocabulary, and unseen yo-go verbs for later lessons.

chapters.title: Poner, Salir, Venir --- Completing the -go Club
chapters.label: ch:completing-go-club
chapters.canDo: I can use the three learned singular forms of poner, salir, and venir and compare their yo forms with tengo, hago, and digo.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C13-practice, the canonical closing checkpoint, and demonstrate the chapter promise with known words and only the learned singular person frame.
payoff.note: The payoff retrieves all nine Chapter-13 atoms and deliberately leaves plural persons, full boot diagrams, reflexive clothing, house and table nouns, clock times, dinner vocabulary, and unseen yo-go verbs for later lessons.

chapters.title: The Preterite --- Your First Past Tense
chapters.label: ch:preterite
chapters.canDo: I can use the singular completed past of ser or ir and the known regular -ar verb hablar.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C14-practice and distinguish fui/fuiste/fue from hablé/hablaste/habló using known words, context, and written stress.
payoff.note: The payoff retrieves all six Chapter-14 atoms with mapped activities and deliberately defers plural persons, other past-tense verb classes, and new time, place, or person vocabulary.

chapters.title: Completing the Preterite --- Three Families, One Question
chapters.label: ch:completing-preterite
chapters.canDo: I can form the singular completed past of regular -er/-ir verbs and the known strong verbs tener, hacer, and estar.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C15-practice and retrieve the bounded singular sets for comer, vivir, tener, hacer, and estar with their spelling and historical contrasts.
payoff.note: The payoff retrieves all twelve Chapter-15 atoms with mapped activities and deliberately defers every plural form, additional irregular verbs, and new time, place, person, or object vocabulary.

chapters.title: The Imperfect --- the Past That Kept Going
chapters.label: ch:imperfect
chapters.canDo: I can use the Spanish imperfect for past habits, background, and actions in progress.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C16-practice and retrieve the bounded singular imperfect rows for hablar, comer, vivir, ser, ir, and newly learned ver while contrasting open and completed past viewpoints.
payoff.note: The payoff retrieves all twelve Chapter-16 atoms with mapped activities and deliberately defers every plural form, undeclared time clue, new person, and new setting.

chapters.title: The Future and the Conditional --- One Weld, Twice
chapters.label: ch:future-conditional
chapters.canDo: I can form the Spanish future and conditional from the infinitive and use each for its core meaning.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C17-practice and retrieve the bounded singular future and conditional rows for hablar, comer, and vivir plus the learned har-, tendr-, and podr- stems.
payoff.note: The payoff retrieves all twelve Chapter-17 atoms with mapped activities and deliberately defers every plural form, additional irregular stem, auxiliary paradigm, object-pronoun frame, and clock-time conjecture.

chapters.title: The Subjunctive --- the Mood of the Not-Yet-Real
chapters.label: ch:subjunctive
chapters.canDo: I can distinguish an asserted event from a wanted one and use the learned singular present-subjunctive forms after quiero que or ojalá.

payoff.summary: Complete ES-C18-practice and choose asserted versus wanted meaning before retrieving the singular forms of hablar, comer, vivir, querer, poder, and hacer in the two learned trigger frames.
payoff.note: The payoff retrieves all twelve Chapter-18 atoms with mapped activities and deliberately defers plural persons, additional irregular verbs, object pronouns, person nouns, and additional subjunctive triggers.

chapters.title: Yes and No
chapters.label: ch:spanish-basic-responses
chapters.canDo: I can answer yes or no in Spanish and negate a sentence by putting no in front of the verb.

payoff.summary: Answer ¿Hablas inglés? with a bare no, then negate the sentence itself — No hablo inglés — with the same one word doing both jobs.

chapters.title: Lo Siento
chapters.label: ch:spanish-sorry
chapters.canDo: I can apologise in Spanish and choose between lo siento and perdón.

payoff.summary: Say lo siento for regret and perdón for fault or for catching someone's attention, hearing sentir — I feel it — inside the first and dōnāre — to give completely — inside the second.

chapters.title: Days of the Week
chapters.label: ch:spanish-days-of-the-week
chapters.canDo: I can name all seven days of the week in Spanish and say why the last two broke away from the planet names.

payoff.summary: Run lunes to domingo straight through, then pair each weekend day against its English twin — sábado against Saturn's day, domingo against the Sun's.

chapters.title: Black, White, Red, and Blue
chapters.label: ch:spanish-black-white-red-blue
chapters.canDo: I can name black, white, red and blue in Spanish and say which of them Spanish borrowed rather than inherited.

payoff.summary: Say negro, blanco, rojo and azul, then sort them by origin: negro inherited from Latin, blanco traditionally linked to the Germanic Visigoths, rojo a cousin of English red by a different Latin branch, and azul carried in from Arabic lāzaward.

chapters.title: Parents and Siblings
chapters.label: ch:spanish-family
chapters.canDo: I can name my parents and my siblings in Spanish and explain why hermano is not built on Latin's word for brother.

payoff.summary: Give el padre, la madre, el hermano and la hermana, trace hermano back through germānus to germen, the seed, rather than to frāter, and separate its silent h from the once-spoken h of hijo and hacer.

chapters.title: Head and Hand
chapters.label: ch:spanish-head-and-hand
chapters.canDo: I can name the head and the hand in Spanish and get la mano's gender right despite its -o ending.

payoff.summary: Say la cabeza and la mano, use me duele la mano, and explain the feminine article on a word that ends in -o by way of Latin's fourth declension.

chapters.title: The Seasons
chapters.label: ch:spanish-seasons
chapters.canDo: I can name the four seasons in Spanish and explain how verano moved from spring to summer.

payoff.summary: Run primavera, verano, otoño, invierno, unpack primavera as prīma vēra, and show verano growing out of that same vēr before its meaning slid across to summer.

chapters.title: Water, Wine, and Bread
chapters.label: ch:spanish-water-wine-bread
chapters.canDo: I can name water, wine and bread in Spanish and say why a compañero is someone who shares bread with me.

payoff.summary: Say el agua, el vino and el pan, then open compañero into com- plus pānis and follow the root out to panadería and panadero.

chapters.title: The Months
chapters.label: ch:spanish-months
chapters.canDo: I can name the twelve months in Spanish and explain why diciembre carries the Latin word for ten.

payoff.summary: Recite enero through diciembre, tie marzo back to martes through Mars, and place septiembre and diciembre against the Roman year that started in March.

chapters.title: Noon and Midnight
chapters.label: ch:spanish-noon-midnight
chapters.canDo: I can say that it is noon or midnight in Spanish and break both words into their two living halves.

payoff.summary: Say es mediodía and es medianoche, split each into medio/media plus día/noche, and set them against French's worn-down midi and minuit.

chapters.title: Telling Time
chapters.label: ch:spanish-telling-time
chapters.canDo: I can tell the time in Spanish and choose correctly between es la una and son las dos.

payoff.summary: Say es la una, son las dos, son las diez, and explain why one o'clock takes a singular verb while every other hour takes a plural one.

chapters.title: The Weather
chapters.label: ch:spanish-weather
chapters.canDo: I can talk about the weather in Spanish and know why llueve refuses to join hace.

payoff.summary: Ask about el tiempo, answer hace calor, hace frío, hace sol, then switch to llueve — a verb of its own, whose ll- is the same sound change that gave llamar.

chapters.title: Numbers Eleven to Twenty
chapters.label: ch:spanish-numbers-eleven-to-twenty
chapters.canDo: I can count from eleven to twenty in Spanish and say where the fused Latin teens stop and the ten-and-X ones begin.

payoff.summary: Run once to quince as fused Latin compounds, then dieciséis to diecinueve as a ten-and-X template, say why Latin's own subtractive 18 and 19 did not survive, and close on veinte.

chapters.title: Dog and Cat
chapters.label: ch:spanish-dog-and-cat
chapters.canDo: I can name a dog and a cat in Spanish and say which of the two words still has no agreed origin.

payoff.summary: Say gato and perro, trace cattus back toward Egypt, then admit that perro — which pushed out the older can — has no settled etymology at all.

chapters.title: Green and Yellow
chapters.label: ch:spanish-green-and-yellow
chapters.canDo: I can name green and yellow in Spanish and explain why amarillo is built on the word for bitter.

payoff.summary: Say verde and amarillo, tie verde to virēre, to flourish, and amarillo to amarellus, a little bitter — the same root as everyday amargo.

chapters.title: Four Verbs of the Mind
chapters.label: ch:spanish-verbs-of-the-mind
chapters.canDo: I can say what I think, understand, read and write in Spanish, and break the stems of pensar and entender the way a stem-changer requires.

payoff.summary: Run pensar and entender through the e→ie boot, then leer and escribir as the pair that does not break, and close on the propped-up e- that turns scrībere into escribir and schola into escuela.

chapters.title: Taking, Asking, Helping — and the Backwards Verb
chapters.label: ch:spanish-backwards-verb
chapters.canDo: I can say I take, ask and help in Spanish, and build a sentence with gustar the way Spanish actually builds it — with the thing liked as the subject.

payoff.summary: Say tomar, preguntar and ayudar, then turn gustar around: me gusta el libro is the book pleasing me, so the verb agrees with the thing and the person moves into the little word in front.

chapters.title: Hearing, Sleeping, Walking, Running
chapters.label: ch:spanish-hear-sleep-walk-run
chapters.canDo: I can say I hear, sleep, walk and run in Spanish, write oír's y where the spelling demands it, and break dormir's o to ue the way a boot verb does.

payoff.summary: Run the chapter's four verbs together and sort them by what they do to their stems: correr, caminar and andar leave theirs alone, dormir breaks o to ue, oír grows a g in oigo and writes y in oyes. Then name each verb's source in turn — audīre, dormīre, Gaulish camminus, currere — and set the two words with no settled origin, andar and perro, against them.

chapters.title: Opening, Closing, Sitting Down, Standing Up
chapters.label: ch:spanish-open-close-sit-stand
chapters.canDo: I can say I open, close, sit down and stand up in Spanish, and use the reflexive pronoun that makes sentarse and levantarse land the action back on me.

payoff.summary: Say the chapter in one breath — abro el libro, me siento, cierro el libro, me levanto — then separate the two features it taught: sentarse is reflexive and a stem-changer, levantarse is reflexive only. Name the shared recipe behind both body-position verbs (a Latin present participle, sedēns and levāns), pick abierto out as the one irregular participle, and reach back to la mano for why the article stays feminine.

chapters.title: Telling What Happened
chapters.label: ch:spanish-narrating
chapters.canDo: I can tell a short connected story about something that happened — ordering the events with luego, giving a reason with porque, and choosing the imperfect for the scene and the preterite for the events.

payoff.summary: Tell a four-sentence story out loud: Llovía. Me levanté, luego bebí café. No corrí, porque llovía mucho. Me senté y leí. Every word in it has been taught in this book, and the two pasts divide the work between scene and event.

chapters.title: Bringing, Getting, Playing, Meeting
chapters.label: ch:spanish-bring-get-play-meet
chapters.canDo: I can say I bring, get, play and meet in Spanish, and name what each verb does to its yo-form or its stem: traigo grows a hard g, consigo breaks e to i and drops a silent u, juego breaks u to ue alone in the language, and conozco keeps a cluster the other forms lost.

payoff.summary: Run the chapter's four verbs in the yo-form — traigo, consigo, juego, conozco — and say what each one does to itself, then name its Latin root and what that root meant: trahere to drag, cōnsequī to follow, iocārī to joke, cognōscere to begin to know. Choose conocer for a person and saber for a fact, and say which of the four carries a thing toward you rather than away. The chapter also reaches back for oigo, the yo-form that first grew a hard g, and for padre beside English father, the model for saying that Spanish and English words can be siblings rather than borrowings.

chapters.title: Waiting, Answering, Buying
chapters.label: ch:spanish-wait-answer-buy
chapters.canDo: I can say I wait, answer and buy in Spanish — three verbs whose endings never surprise me — and I know that esperar alone carries wait, hope and expect, so context does the work English hands to three separate verbs.

payoff.summary: Run espero, contesto and compro — three verbs that break nothing, whose whole difficulty is meaning — and give each root and its sense: spērāre to hope, contestārī to call witnesses, comparāre to procure. Refuse the lookalike: English compare descends from a different Latin comparāre built on compār, so it is not a relative. Then buy — compro el pan, el vino y un café, por favor — and reach back for what pānis gave compañero, which English words vīnum reached, why café is masculine, and what por favor says word for word.

chapters.title: Saying Why
chapters.label: ch:spanish-giving-reasons
chapters.canDo: I can give a reason for what I think and what I plan — stating an opinion with creo que, running forward to its consequence with así que, and naming an obligation with debo.

payoff.summary: Answer ¿Por qué no corres? in four moves — Creo que llueve. No corro porque llueve, así que leo. Debo estudiar. Opinion, cause, consequence, obligation, each with its own word, and every word in it taught by this book.
